# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

MLflow is a lab notebook that the code writes. Every time a training or an
analysis runs, it records what went in, what came out, and the files it made,
so that runs can be compared later and every result leads back to the run that
produced it. It records only what the code tells it, and only where the code
tells it to; almost everything that goes wrong with MLflow follows from that
(@sec-model). Working with it comes down to logging runs, comparing them, and
logging and loading models (@sec-usage).

MLflow is written in Python and logs from Python; R and Java have clients as
well. Besides tracking, MLflow 3 traces and evaluates applications built on
large language models, which this document leaves out.

Checked against MLflow 3.17.


# How MLflow thinks {#sec-model}

MLflow keeps its records in a tracking store, which holds experiments, the
experiments hold runs, and a run holds four kinds of records. A separate
registry gives names and versions to the models that runs produced:

```default
tracking store             mlflow.db, or a tracking server
    experiment             "melting-point": the runs of one question
        run                one execution of the code, such as one training
            parameters     what went in:      learning_rate=0.01, seed=42
            metrics        what came out:     val_loss at steps 0, 1, 2, ...
            artifacts      the files it made: model/, residuals.png
            tags           notes:             git commit, user, run name
    registered model       "melting-point"
        version 1          a model logged by a run; alias "champion"
```

A run is the unit of everything: it has a status, `RUNNING`, `FINISHED`, or
`FAILED`, and an ID by which a result names the run that produced it.


## Parameters, metrics, artifacts, and tags {#sec-records}

Parameters are what went into a run, such as hyperparameters, the seed, and the
path of the data. A parameter is set once per run and cannot change its value
afterwards, and it is stored as text: `0.01` comes back as the string `"0.01"`,
and a sort of parameters puts `"10"` before `"9"`. Convert them to numbers
before comparing them.

Metrics are numbers that came out of a run, and each can be logged many times,
with a step, such as the loss after every epoch, which the user interface
shows as a curve. Artifacts are files, such as a trained model, a plot, or a
table of predictions, and are stored apart from the other records, in an
artifact store. Tags are notes, such as a description, and MLflow sets some
itself: the user, the script, and the commit of the code.


## It records only what the code tells it {#sec-only-what-logged}

MLflow knows nothing that the code does not log. A seed that is not logged, an
input file named only by its path, and a default of a library that was not
passed explicitly are all missing from the run, and two runs that differ only
in them look the same. Log every parameter that the result depends on,
including the defaults and the seed
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)), and the data with
`log_input`, which stores a digest of their contents (@sec-log). Autologging
logs the parameters of the model, with its defaults, but neither the data nor
the seeds of the code around it (@sec-autolog).

MLflow tags a run with the commit of the Git repository it was started from,
but it does not check whether the code has uncommitted changes. A run started
from a changed working tree carries the commit of code that never ran.
Commit before a run that counts, or log the output of `git diff` as an
artifact.


## Where the records go {#sec-store}

The tracking URI says where the records go. Without one, MLflow writes into a
SQLite database `mlflow.db` and a directory `mlruns/` for the artifacts, in the
current working directory: a script started from another directory writes
into another database, and the earlier runs seem to be gone. Set the tracking
URI explicitly, to an absolute path or a server (@sec-log).

A SQLite database is one file, written by one process at a time. On the network
file systems of clusters, its locking is unreliable, and many jobs that log at
once should log to a tracking server instead (@sec-server), which also lets a
team share its runs.

A run whose process is killed, such as a job that exceeds its time or memory
limit, never ends: it stays `RUNNING` for good, with the metrics up to the
moment it was killed. Compare only runs with the status `FINISHED`
(@sec-compare). A run that ends with an exception in a `with` block is marked
`FAILED`.


## Models and the registry {#sec-registry}

A logged model is a directory of artifacts: the model in the format of its
library, a file `MLmodel` that says how to load it, the packages it needs, in
`requirements.txt` and `conda.yaml`, and an example of its input. Any logged
model loads as a generic model with a `predict` method, whatever library made
it.

The registry gives a model a name and numbered versions, each a model logged by
some run, and aliases, such as `champion`, that point to a version. Code that
loads `models:/melting-point@champion` gets whichever version the alias points
to today, which can change tomorrow, like the tag of a container image
([](../containers/index.qmd#sec-record)). Record the number of the version with
the results, not the alias.


# Working with MLflow {#sec-usage}

The examples log a model that predicts melting points. The same functions log
any computation whose runs are worth comparing, such as a simulation or a fit.


## Log a run {#sec-log}

```python
import mlflow

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("sqlite:////project/ocean/mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_experiment("melting-point")

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="baseline"):
    mlflow.log_params({"learning_rate": 0.01, "n_layers": 3, "seed": 42})
    data = mlflow.data.from_pandas(train, source="data/train.parquet")
    mlflow.log_input(data, context="training")
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", train_one_epoch(), step=epoch)
    mlflow.log_artifact("residuals.png")
```

A SQLite URI takes three slashes before a relative path and four before an
absolute one, as here. The environment variable `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` sets the
URI without changing the code, such as in a job script. `set_experiment`
creates the experiment if it does not exist. The `with` block ends the run, as
`FINISHED` or, after an exception, as `FAILED`.


## Log automatically {#sec-autolog}

```python
mlflow.sklearn.autolog()
model = Ridge(alpha=0.5).fit(X_train, y_train)   # logged as a run
```

Autologging, for scikit-learn, PyTorch Lightning, XGBoost, and other
libraries, or `mlflow.autolog()` for all of them, logs the parameters of the
model, including its defaults, the metrics of the training, and the model
itself, without a call in the code. It logs what the library sees, not the
data or the seeds of the code around it (@sec-only-what-logged), and it logs
the model even when the code logs it as well, unless `log_models=False`.


## Compare runs {#sec-compare}

```python
runs = mlflow.search_runs(
    experiment_names=["melting-point"],
    filter_string="attributes.status = 'FINISHED' and metrics.val_loss < 0.1",
    order_by=["metrics.val_loss ASC"],
)
```

`search_runs` returns a table of pandas, with a row per run and columns such as
`params.seed`, `metrics.val_loss`, and `tags.mlflow.source.git.commit`, for
analysis in code. `mlflow ui`, started in the directory of `mlflow.db`, or with
`--backend-store-uri`, shows the runs in a browser at `http://localhost:5000`,
with their curves side by side. A run left `RUNNING` by a killed process can be
marked with `MlflowClient().set_terminated(run_id, status="KILLED")`.


## Log, register, and load a model {#sec-models}

```python
from mlflow import MlflowClient

info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", input_example=X_train[:5])
version = mlflow.register_model(info.model_uri, "melting-point")
MlflowClient().set_registered_model_alias(
    "melting-point", "champion", version.version
)

model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/melting-point@champion")
```

`log_model` logs the model inside the current run, and `register_model` makes
it a new version of a registered model. `pyfunc.load_model` loads any model
with a `predict` method, whatever library made it; `mlflow.sklearn.load_model`
loads the original object of scikit-learn. A model loads by its version as
well, as `models:/melting-point/1`.


## Run a tracking server {#sec-server}

```bash
mlflow server \
    --backend-store-uri postgresql://mlflow@db.lab.example/mlflow \
    --artifacts-destination s3://lab-mlflow-artifacts \
    --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5000
```

A tracking server keeps the records of a team, or of many jobs, in a database,
such as PostgreSQL, and the artifacts in a store, such as a bucket of S3
([](../cloud/aws.qmd#sec-s3)). The clients set their tracking URI to its
address, such as `http://mlflow.lab.example:5000`, and send everything through
it. The server answers only on the machine itself, unless `--host` names
another address, and by default it asks for no login: start it with
`--app-name basic-auth` for users and passwords, put it behind a web server
that asks for them, or reach it through an SSH tunnel.
